question: Which statement best describes Urgent vs non-urgent updates?
options: Concurrent rendering splits state updates into two priority lanes. Urgent updates (typing into an input, clicking a button, selecting an item) must reflect immediately and take the express lane. Non-urgent updates (re-rendering a huge filtered list derived from that input) can lag a frame or two without hurting UX, so React renders them in an interruptible background lane. Choosing the right lane for each update is the whole game.

isPending is a boolean from useTransition that is true while the transition is still rendering in the background. It exists so you can show a subtle loading affordance, dimming the stale results or showing a 'Updating…' label, without blocking the urgent update. It gives users feedback that newer results are on the way while the current ones stay interactive.

useDeferredValue takes a value and returns a copy that lags behind during heavy work, re-rendering at transition priority once urgent work settles. Reach for it when you do not own the setter, for example a value arrives as a prop, so you cannot wrap the update. You feed the deferred value into the expensive computation while the live value updates the input immediately.

useTransition returns [isPending, startTransition]. Wrapping a setter in startTransition marks that update as a transition, so React schedules it at low priority and lets urgent updates jump ahead. The critical rule: only the expensive setter goes inside; the urgent update that drives the controlled input must stay outside, or typing itself becomes laggy.

Deferring a value only helps if the expensive child can skip re-rendering when that value hasn't changed. If the heavy subtree re-renders on every parent render regardless, deferral does nothing. Wrap the heavy component in React.memo and feed it the deferred value, or compute the expensive result with useMemo keyed on the deferred value, so an unchanged value genuinely bails out.

Debouncing delays work by a fixed timer for everyone, even on fast devices, and cannot interrupt a render already underway. Transitions adapt to actual load: they yield to urgent input and restart automatically, so the experience scales with the user's hardware. Concurrent Hooks remove the need for many manual debounce/throttle hacks while expressing intent declaratively.
